(CNN) — Few figures have dominated sumo as powerfully—or generated as much controversy—as Asashoryu. The 330-pound Mongolian became the sport’s most accomplished grand champion, yet even his achievements could not overshadow the scandals and tragedies that had troubled Japan’s national sport in recent years.

Born Dolgorsuren Dagvadorj, Asashoryu was raised in Mongolia in a wrestling family: his father and two older brothers were successful competitors. He later went to Japan as a student, where he was recruited and coached by the Takasago stable. In 1999, at age 18, he entered professional sumo.

His rapid climb through the ranks included his first tournament, or basho, victory in 2002. In January 2003, he reached sumo’s highest rank, becoming a grand champion, or yokozuna. He was only the 68th wrestler to earn that title in the sport’s 2,000-year history. Two years afterward, he made history again as the first and only man to win all six official tournaments held in a single year.

Many observers believed Asashoryu’s spectacular ascent brought new energy to a sport suffering from declining popularity and a shortage of successful Japanese-born wrestlers. Nevertheless, his dominance inside the dohyo did not appeal to everyone. Critics said his victories had become overly predictable, while traditionalists argued that he lacked “hinkaku”—the composure and dignity required of a yokozuna—and failed to show sufficient respect for sumo’s customs.

In 2003, officials disqualified him from a match after he grabbed an opponent’s topknot. Incidents such as that helped establish his reputation as sumo’s enfant terrible.

Debate over Asashoryu’s conduct was only one part of a broader crisis. A succession of controversies damaged sumo’s image as a dignified, tradition-bound sport and demonstrated that it was vulnerable to many of the same problems affecting other sports. Because sumo’s place in Japanese culture dates back to its role in Shinto religious ceremonies, its difficulties came close to creating a crisis of national identity.

In September, three foreign wrestlers were expelled for using recreational drugs. The episode prompted Kitanoumi, the sport’s chairman and a former wrestler, to resign. It followed several years of match-fixing accusations, some of which directly involved Asashoryu, and pushed sumo into another period of turmoil. In January 2007, he was accused of paying other wrestlers to deliberately lose matches, reinforcing perceptions that corruption was widespread.

Asashoryu encountered further trouble later in 2007. The sumo federation suspended him for allegedly falsifying a doctor’s note and ordered him to remain at his Tokyo home. Reports subsequently suggested that he had suffered a nervous breakdown.

Reaching the top of sumo requires psychological resilience as well as physical power. Although the sport’s grueling training and stable “hazing” practices had long been acknowledged and tolerated, they were linked to a tragedy earlier that year. Takashi Saito, a 17-year-old sumo apprentice, died in horrific circumstances after allegedly being beaten to death by his stable master and three fellow wrestlers.

For the remainder of the year, Asashoryu’s objective was to continue asserting himself in the dohyo, while sumo itself sought to regain its balance and dignity.

# From Mongolian Prodigy to Embattled Champion: Asashoryu and Sumo’s Crisis of Trust

**TOKYO —** When Asashoryu strode into the raised ring, slapped his belt and fixed his opponent with a hard stare, he looked like the future of sumo wrestling: fast, powerful and unapologetically confident.

Born Dolgorsürengiin Dagvadorj in Ulaanbaatar in 1980, Asashoryu arrived in Japan as a teenager and entered professional sumo in 1999. His ascent was extraordinarily quick. He reached the sport’s second-highest rank, ozeki, in 2002 and was promoted to yokozuna in January 2003, becoming the first Mongolian to attain sumo’s supreme title.

His promotion marked a turning point. Japan’s ancient national sport had already embraced champions from Hawaii, but Asashoryu demonstrated that Mongolia could become one of sumo’s great recruiting grounds. Compact by heavyweight standards but exceptionally athletic, he relied on balance, speed and a broad range of throwing and grappling techniques.

At his peak, he was nearly untouchable. In 2005, he became the first wrestler to win all six top-division tournaments in a calendar year. By the time his career ended, he had collected 25 championships, then the third-highest total in history.

Yet Asashoryu’s rise also exposed a tension at the heart of modern sumo: whether its greatest stars were merely athletes or custodians of a rigid cultural tradition.

A yokozuna cannot be demoted. He is instead expected to retire when his results—or his conduct—fall below the dignity associated with the rank. Asashoryu’s aggression and exuberance thrilled many spectators, but critics said his celebrations, occasional outbursts and confrontational manner violated that standard.

The conflict came to a head in 2007. After withdrawing from a regional tour with medical complaints, Asashoryu was filmed playing in a charity soccer match in Mongolia. The Japan Sumo Association suspended him for two tournaments and cut his pay. Supporters said the punishment was excessive; traditionalists argued that he had dishonored the duties of a yokozuna.

His career ended in 2010 after allegations that he assaulted a man during a night out in Tokyo. Asashoryu retired amid intense pressure from sumo authorities. The episode cemented his reputation as both a transformative champion and a figure who never fully accommodated himself to the behavioral expectations imposed on the sport’s highest rank.

But his downfall was only one part of a far broader crisis.

In 2007, 17-year-old trainee Takashi Saito, known in sumo as Tokitaizan, died after being beaten during what was presented as disciplinary training at the Tokitsukaze stable. The stablemaster and several wrestlers were later convicted. The case exposed a brutal side of sumo’s closed stable system, in which young recruits lived under near-total control of senior wrestlers and coaches. Practices long defended as tough instruction came under scrutiny as possible hazing and abuse.

The following year, marijuana cases further damaged the sport. Russian wrestler Wakanoho was arrested for cannabis possession, while brothers Roho and Hakurozan were dismissed after testing positive, though they disputed the findings. These incidents were separate from Asashoryu, who was not implicated in the drug cases, but they reinforced an image of an organization struggling to police its wrestlers.

The gravest institutional blow came in 2011, after police investigating an unrelated matter found mobile-phone messages that appeared to document planned results and payments between wrestlers. The evidence confirmed that at least some bouts had been manipulated, turning decades of rumors about match-fixing into an official scandal.

The Sumo Association canceled the March grand tournament, the first cancellation over scandal in modern sumo, and forced numerous wrestlers and coaches from the sport. Asashoryu was not implicated in that investigation, having retired the previous year. Nevertheless, the revelations cast a shadow over the era in which he had competed by raising doubts about the integrity of sumo’s central spectacle.

Together, the controversies attacked every part of the sport’s public identity. Misconduct cases undermined the claim that champions embodied exceptional dignity. Drug incidents challenged sumo’s insistence on discipline. Hazing exposed the dangers hidden behind stable walls. Match-fixing threatened the most basic promise made to spectators: that the contest in the ring was genuine.

Sumo has since introduced compliance measures, outside oversight and reforms intended to protect recruits and restore trust. It has also become increasingly international, with Mongolian-born yokozuna including Hakuho, Harumafuji, Kakuryu and Terunofuji following the path Asashoryu helped establish.

Asashoryu remains a complicated figure in that history. His brilliance accelerated sumo’s globalization and inspired a generation of Mongolian wrestlers. His turbulent exit, however, became emblematic of a sport caught between athletic celebrity and ceremonial expectation.

The scandals that surrounded sumo during and after his reign cannot fairly be attributed to him alone. But they transformed the way the public viewed the institution he dominated. The dohyo was no longer simply a sacred arena occupied by larger-than-life champions. It was also the center of a closed system whose traditions, discipline and claims to honor had begun to face unprecedented scrutiny.

# Asashoryu: The Mongolian Champion Who Transformed—and Troubled—Sumo

**Dolgorsürengiin Dagvadorj** (Mongolian: Долгорсүрэнгийн Дагвадорж), better known by his ring name **Asashoryu Akinori**, is a retired Mongolian sumo wrestler who became the **68th yokozuna**, or grand champion, of Japanese professional sumo. Fiercely athletic, technically versatile, and intensely competitive, he won **25 top-division championships** and was the sport’s dominant figure for much of the 2000s.

Asashoryu was also one of sumo’s most polarizing champions. His emotional celebrations, confrontational behavior, disciplinary problems, and uneasy relationship with the customs expected of a yokozuna repeatedly generated controversy. To admirers, he was a charismatic competitor who revived public interest in sumo and opened the way for a generation of Mongolian stars. To critics, he failed to demonstrate the dignity and restraint traditionally associated with the sport’s highest rank.

## Early life in Mongolia

Dagvadorj was born on **September 27, 1980, in Ulaanbaatar, Mongolia**, into a family with a strong background in Mongolian wrestling. His father was an accomplished practitioner of **bökh**, Mongolia’s traditional form of wrestling, and several of his brothers also became prominent athletes. His older brother Dolgorsürengiin Sumyaabazar competed in wrestling and later entered Mongolian politics.

Dagvadorj grew up practicing wrestling and other sports in a culture where successful wrestlers often become national celebrities. Although Mongolian wrestling differs significantly from sumo—there is no ring-out rule, for example—it gave him balance, leverage, body awareness, and experience in close physical combat.

As a teenager, he went to Japan and attended **Meitoku Gijuku High School** in Kochi Prefecture, a school known for recruiting and developing athletes. There he trained in amateur sumo before entering the professional ranks.

## Entry into professional sumo

Dagvadorj joined **Wakamatsu stable**, later absorbed into or renamed **Takasago stable**, and made his professional debut in **January 1999**. He received the ring name **Asashoryu**, commonly translated as “Morning Blue Dragon.” The “Asa” element reflected his stable’s naming tradition, while “shoryu” evoked the image of a rising or blue dragon.

He advanced with exceptional speed:

- **Professional debut:** January 1999  
- **Promotion to juryo:** September 2000  
- **Top-division debut:** January 2001  
- **Promotion to ozeki:** 2002  
- **Promotion to yokozuna:** January 2003  

After winning consecutive top-division tournaments in **November 2002** and **January 2003**, Asashoryu was promoted to yokozuna. He became the first Mongolian—and the third foreign-born wrestler after Akebono and Musashimaru—to reach sumo’s highest rank.

His promotion was historically significant. Mongolia had already begun supplying Japan with talented wrestlers, but Asashoryu proved that a Mongolian could become not merely successful but the central figure in the sport.

## Wrestling style

Asashoryu was relatively light for a yokozuna of his era, generally competing at around 145 kilograms rather than relying on extraordinary bulk. His strength lay in speed, balance, explosiveness, and tactical adaptability.

He could win by:

- Powerful frontal charges
- Belt throws and trips rooted partly in Mongolian wrestling
- Rapid lateral movement
- Leg techniques
- Force-outs and push-outs
- Sudden changes of direction
- Counterattacks from apparently losing positions

Unlike wrestlers who depended on one preferred grip or a narrow range of techniques, Asashoryu was difficult to prepare for. He could fight effectively both on and away from the mawashi, sumo’s ceremonial belt. His reflexes and low center of gravity frequently allowed him to survive at the edge of the ring and reverse an opponent’s attack.

His style was also psychological. He stared intensely at opponents, displayed obvious confidence, and approached bouts with a confrontational energy unusual in a sport that formally prizes controlled behavior.

## Championship dominance

Asashoryu won **25 Emperor’s Cups**, the trophies awarded to top-division tournament champions. At the time of his retirement, only Taiho and Chiyonofuji had won more.

Among his major accomplishments were:

- **25 top-division championships**
- **Five undefeated 15–0 championships**
- **Seven consecutive tournament victories**, from November 2004 through November 2005
- Victory in **all six official tournaments held in 2005**
- An **84–6 record in 2005**, then the best single calendar-year performance in modern six-tournament sumo
- A career record generally listed as **669 wins, 173 losses, and 76 absences**
- A top-division record of **596 wins, 153 losses, and 76 absences**

His 2005 season was particularly extraordinary. No wrestler had previously won all six top-division tournaments in a calendar year. His 84 victories out of a possible 90 established a benchmark that symbolized the scale of his dominance.

For part of his reign, Asashoryu was the only active yokozuna. That left him as sumo’s most visible representative and placed extraordinary pressure on him to embody both athletic supremacy and the ceremonial ideals of the rank.

His chief rivals included Kaio, Chiyotaikai, Tochiazuma, Kotooshu, and later **Hakuho**, another Mongolian who became yokozuna in 2007. The emergence of Hakuho produced a compelling rivalry and ended Asashoryu’s period of largely unchallenged control. Hakuho later surpassed all previous championship records, but Asashoryu had helped create the environment in which Mongolian wrestlers could dominate the sport.

## Expectations placed on a yokozuna

A yokozuna cannot be demoted for poor performance. Instead, he is expected to retire when he can no longer compete at the required level. In return for that privilege, he is held to a standard known as **hinkaku**, usually translated as dignity, grace, or character.

Hinkaku is deliberately broad. It includes not only conduct during bouts but also public behavior, respect for ritual, emotional restraint, and willingness to represent sumo as a cultural institution.

This was the source of much of the conflict surrounding Asashoryu. His supporters argued that some criticism reflected discomfort with a foreign champion who was outspoken and unwilling to suppress his personality. His critics responded that every yokozuna, regardless of nationality, was required to meet standards stricter than those applied to ordinary athletes.

## Early controversies

Asashoryu’s competitive intensity often carried beyond the instant a bout was decided. He was criticized for giving unnecessary extra shoves, glaring at opponents, celebrating too openly, and appearing insufficiently respectful after victories.

In 2003, he was disqualified from a bout against fellow Mongolian **Kyokushuzan** for pulling his opponent’s topknot, an illegal act in sumo. It was an embarrassing and extremely unusual result for a yokozuna. The two wrestlers also had a strained relationship, contributing to the perception that Asashoryu brought personal emotion into the ring.

He was repeatedly warned over etiquette, including the way he accepted prize money and performed ceremonial actions. Some incidents were minor in isolation, but together they reinforced a public image of a champion unwilling—or unable—to conform fully to sumo’s traditions.

## The 2007 soccer scandal and suspension

The most serious disciplinary episode before his retirement occurred in 2007. Asashoryu withdrew from a regional sumo tour after submitting medical documentation for injuries. He then returned to Mongolia and was filmed participating in a charity soccer event.

The footage caused an uproar in Japan. Even if he did not play at full intensity, his appearance on a soccer field seemed inconsistent with the injuries that had excused him from official duties.

The Japan Sumo Association suspended him for **two tournaments**, reduced his salary, and placed him under restrictions that effectively confined him to his home and stable. The punishment was unprecedentedly severe for a yokozuna.

The episode appeared to affect him psychologically. Reports indicated that he suffered symptoms associated with severe stress or depression, and he was eventually allowed to return to Mongolia for treatment. When he came back to competition in January 2008, public attention was intense. Although he lost the championship-deciding bout to Hakuho, he later won the March 2008 tournament, demonstrating that he remained capable of competing at the highest level.

## Final scandal and retirement

Asashoryu revived his career in 2009, winning two championships, and captured his **25th and final title in January 2010**. Yet almost immediately, reports emerged that he had been involved in a late-night, alcohol-related altercation outside a Tokyo nightclub during the tournament.

Early accounts suggested a dispute with a manager or associate; later reports alleged that Asashoryu had assaulted another man. Details were contested, and the incident did not proceed to a definitive public criminal judgment establishing every allegation. Nevertheless, the Sumo Association viewed the episode as the culmination of a long pattern of misconduct.

On **February 4, 2010**, Asashoryu announced his retirement at the age of 29. He apologized for causing trouble and said he had accepted responsibility. Although technically described as a voluntary retirement, it was widely understood that he had faced intense pressure from sumo authorities and that expulsion was possible had he refused.

His departure was abrupt. He had just won a championship and was still one of the strongest wrestlers in the sport. Few yokozuna have retired while remaining so competitively relevant.

## Life after sumo

After retirement, Dagvadorj returned frequently to Mongolia and became involved in business, sports promotion, charity, and public life. He remained a major celebrity in both Mongolia and Japan. He also continued to comment on sumo and occasionally appeared in Japanese media.

Unlike many retired Japanese wrestlers, he did not become a long-term elder within the Japan Sumo Association. Entry into the elder system traditionally requires Japanese citizenship, among other conditions, and Asashoryu retained his Mongolian identity and pursued interests outside the association.

His formal retirement ceremony took place later in 2010 and included the ceremonial cutting of his topknot, marking the end of his professional sumo career.

## Impact on Japanese sumo

Asashoryu’s influence on sumo was both athletic and cultural.

### Establishing Mongolian dominance

He was the first Mongolian yokozuna and the first Mongolian to dominate sumo over an extended period. His success encouraged scouts and stables to recruit more heavily from Mongolia. Hakuho, Harumafuji, Kakuryu, and Terunofuji later became yokozuna, making Mongolian wrestlers central to 21st-century sumo.

Asashoryu did not begin Mongolian participation in the sport, but he transformed its scale and meaning. After him, Mongolian wrestlers were no longer viewed merely as promising foreigners; they were seen as potential grand champions.

### Reviving public interest

Sumo entered the early 2000s facing injuries and retirements among major Japanese stars, especially after the end of the celebrated Takanohana era. Asashoryu’s speed, emotion, and unpredictability gave the sport a compelling central personality.

Even people who disliked him often watched because of him. His bouts carried drama, and his rivalry with Hakuho helped sustain interest during a period of broader concern over sumo’s popularity and institutional problems.

### Redefining the image of a champion

Asashoryu challenged the conventional image of a yokozuna as emotionally restrained and ceremonially flawless. He behaved more like a modern international sports superstar: expressive, combative, proud, and openly eager to defeat rivals.

That made him attractive to younger and overseas audiences, but it also exposed the tension between sumo as competitive entertainment and sumo as a guardian of Japanese tradition.

### Provoking debate about nationality and tradition

Criticism of Asashoryu cannot be reduced simply to prejudice; many of his disciplinary problems were genuine and serious. At the same time, the intensity of the reaction to his behavior generated debate over whether foreign wrestlers were judged more harshly or expected to demonstrate a particularly strict form of cultural assimilation.

His career therefore became a lens through which Japan discussed identity, immigration, sportsmanship, and who had the right to embody a national tradition.

## Legacy

Asashoryu remains one of the greatest and most controversial wrestlers in sumo history. His **25 championships**, seven consecutive tournament victories, and unprecedented sweep of all six tournaments in 2005 place him among the sport’s elite competitors.

His legacy, however, cannot be separated from the incidents that ended his career. He repeatedly struggled with the ceremonial and behavioral obligations of yokozuna status, and his final retirement came not because of declining ability but because sumo’s governing authorities concluded that his conduct had become incompatible with the rank.

That contradiction explains his enduring fascination. Asashoryu was at once a transformative champion and an institutional problem: a wrestler who mastered nearly every physical aspect of sumo while resisting—or failing to satisfy—some of its deepest social expectations. He helped internationalize Japan’s national sport, inspired the rise of Mongolian champions, and forced sumo to confront the tension between tradition and global competition.

counterfactuals.prompt: Draft a sports-news analysis portraying Asashoryu as both one of sumo’s greatest champions and its enfant terrible, while placing his story in the context of sumo’s recent scandals and identity crisis.
counterfactuals.output:
**Asashoryu’s complicated legacy still looms over sumo’s identity crisis**

Few wrestlers embodied sumo’s contradictions as completely as Asashoryu Akinori. The Mongolian-born yokozuna was both one of the sport’s greatest champions and its enduring *enfant terrible*: a ferocious competitor whose 25 top-division titles place him among the most successful wrestlers in history, but whose repeated clashes with sumo’s customs helped bring his career to a premature end.

At his peak, Asashoryu transformed the ring into a display of speed, aggression and improvisation. He became the first Mongolian promoted to yokozuna, sumo’s highest rank, in 2003 and for several years stood alone at the summit. Smaller than many rivals, he compensated with exceptional balance, technique and competitive instinct. In 2005 he won all six major tournaments—a feat unprecedented in the modern six-tournament era—and finished the year with 84 victories from 90 regulation bouts.

Those achievements make any assessment of Asashoryu impossible without the language of greatness. Yet his dominance was accompanied by a mounting catalogue of controversies. He was criticized for visible anger, rough conduct after bouts and a perceived disregard for the dignity expected of a yokozuna. In 2007, he was suspended after withdrawing from regional exhibitions with reported injuries and then appearing in televised footage playing soccer in Mongolia. In early 2010, allegations that he had assaulted a man during a night out in Tokyo prompted intense pressure from the Japan Sumo Association. He retired soon afterward, at 29.

The reaction revealed how much more is demanded of a yokozuna than winning. The rank carries no possibility of demotion; failure is answered by retirement. Its holders are expected to exhibit *hinkaku*—often translated as dignity or grace—an elastic ideal shaped as much by social expectations as by performance.

Asashoryu’s supporters argued that those expectations were applied selectively and that a foreign champion was judged not only on his behavior but on how convincingly he conformed to a deeply Japanese institution. His critics countered that his nationality was irrelevant: a yokozuna who repeatedly embarrassed the sport had failed in the rank’s central duty.

That debate has only become more significant as sumo has confronted a series of scandals. A 17-year-old trainee died in 2007 after violent hazing, exposing brutality inside the stable system. Illegal gambling cases shook the sport in 2010. The following year, evidence of match-fixing led to the cancellation of a major tournament. In 2017, Mongolian yokozuna Harumafuji retired after assaulting a lower-ranked wrestler, while later abuse cases and disciplinary disputes continued to challenge the association’s claims of reform.

Together, those episodes exposed an institution caught between sacred tradition, professional sport and modern demands for transparency. Sumo presents itself as a guardian of ritual and hierarchy, yet its closed stable culture has sometimes protected practices that would be intolerable elsewhere. Its governing body has often appeared quicker to police public decorum than to confront misconduct behind closed doors.

That is why Asashoryu’s story remains relevant. He was not merely a rebel victimized by an inflexible establishment; his behavior repeatedly tested reasonable boundaries, and the allegations surrounding his final days were serious. But he also became a convenient symbol of disorder at a time when sumo’s deeper problems were institutional rather than individual.

Foreign-born wrestlers, particularly Mongolians, have since become central to elite sumo. Their success has expanded the sport’s reach while sharpening questions about identity: Is sumo a Japanese cultural inheritance to which outsiders must assimilate completely, or an international competition whose traditions must evolve with its athletes?

Asashoryu forced that question earlier and more dramatically than anyone. In the ring, he was a master—explosive, inventive and relentlessly ambitious. Outside it, he could be provocative, undisciplined and seemingly indifferent to the restraint his rank demanded.

His legacy therefore resists a clean verdict. He was one of sumo’s defining champions and one of its most disruptive personalities, a wrestler who exposed both the power of the sport’s traditions and the fragility of the institution enforcing them. More than a decade after his retirement, sumo is still wrestling with the contradictions he made impossible to ignore.

counterfactuals.output:
# Asashoryu and the Crisis of Modern Sumo

When Asashoryu entered professional sumo in January 1999, he appeared to embody the sport’s expanding horizons. Born Dolgorsürengiin Dagvadorj in Mongolia, he was fast, technically adventurous and ferociously ambitious. Within four years he had risen from an unknown teenager to yokozuna, sumo’s highest rank.

Yet his career also became a lens through which nearly every anxiety surrounding modern sumo could be seen: the growing dependence on foreign talent, conflict over tradition and identity, weak institutional governance, sensational media coverage, and persistent suspicions that the sport’s results could be manipulated.

Asashoryu did not create these troubles. But his extraordinary ascent—and the controversies that followed—forced sumo to confront them in public.

## A foreign champion rises

Asashoryu arrived in Japan as part of the wave of Mongolian athletes who transformed professional sumo. He joined Takasago stable and made his competitive debut in 1999. Though undersized by the standards of the top division, he compensated with speed, balance and an unusually broad arsenal of throws and trips.

He reached the elite makuuchi division in 2001, became an ozeki in 2002 and, after winning consecutive championships, was promoted in January 2003 as the 68th yokozuna. He was the first Mongolian to hold the rank.

His rise came at an important moment. The popular Japanese-born yokozuna Takanohana had retired, while Akebono and Musashimaru—both born outside Japan—had already demonstrated the internationalization of the sport. Asashoryu soon stood alone at the summit, winning title after title and bringing an intensity that sumo badly needed.

But dominance did not automatically produce affection. The yokozuna is not merely expected to win. He is supposed to represent *hinkaku*, usually translated as dignity, grace or moral character. The term is deliberately vague, allowing officials and commentators to treat conduct outside the ring as part of a champion’s qualifications.

Asashoryu’s aggressive celebrations, flashes of temper and confrontational style were therefore judged as cultural offenses as well as personal faults. Some criticism was justified: he could be reckless, abrasive and disdainful of ceremony. But the reaction also exposed a deeper problem. Sumo was recruiting foreign wrestlers to sustain its competitive strength while expecting them to conform to an unwritten and sometimes inconsistently enforced model of Japanese behavior.

The sport wanted international talent without becoming fully international itself.

## The burden of being the only yokozuna

Asashoryu’s most dominant period came when he was sumo’s sole yokozuna. In 2005 he won all six official tournaments, a feat unprecedented in the six-tournament era. His supremacy was evidence of greatness, but it also revealed the weakness of the field around him.

Sumo’s popularity had declined from the boom years of the 1990s. Fewer Japanese boys were willing to enter a life defined by communal living, rigid hierarchy, low starting pay and punishing physical demands. Baseball, football and other sports offered alternative paths to fame. Meanwhile, wrestlers from Mongolia and elsewhere increasingly occupied the upper ranks.

Foreign wrestlers were sometimes blamed for the absence of Japanese champions, even though their success was partly a consequence of sumo’s domestic recruitment problems. Restrictions were introduced limiting stables to one foreign-born wrestler, but quotas could not solve the deeper issue: the traditional stable system had become less attractive to young Japanese athletes.

Asashoryu was thus both an answer to sumo’s talent shortage and a symbol of it. Every victory strengthened the competition while intensifying fears that the national sport was losing its national character.

## The 2007 suspension

The contradictions became impossible to ignore in 2007.

That summer, Asashoryu withdrew from an official regional exhibition tour, submitting medical diagnoses that included injuries. He then appeared in Mongolia playing in a charity football match. Television footage of the yokozuna running on a field produced an immediate scandal in Japan.

The Japan Sumo Association suspended him for two tournaments, barred him from the regional tour and reduced his salary. It was an extraordinarily severe punishment for a yokozuna and reportedly contributed to a period of serious psychological distress. He was eventually permitted to return to Mongolia for treatment.

To many Japanese fans, the football match proved that Asashoryu had evaded his obligations. Regional tours are not trivial engagements: they promote sumo outside the major cities, generate revenue and allow local supporters to see elite wrestlers. A yokozuna is expected to recognize that duty.

Yet the episode also showed the association’s habitual reliance on punishment rather than transparent administration. There was little public confidence in its procedures for evaluating injuries, handling mental health or distinguishing deliberate deception from poor judgment. Decisions appeared to emerge from closed councils of former wrestlers, guided by custom rather than clearly stated rules.

The controversy became a cultural referendum. Critics depicted Asashoryu as selfish and unworthy of his rank. Defenders saw an injured foreign athlete being made an example of by an institution uncomfortable with his independence. Both interpretations contained elements of truth, but the intensity of the dispute revealed how much sumo had invested in one man. With no other yokozuna until Hakuho’s promotion in 2007, Asashoryu was simultaneously indispensable and perpetually suspect.

## Bribery and match-fixing allegations

Even before the suspension, Asashoryu had faced a more damaging accusation. In 2007, the weekly magazine *Shukan Gendai* published claims that he had paid opponents to lose matches, part of broader allegations of bout-fixing in professional sumo.

Such accusations struck at the sport’s central vulnerability. Sumo presents itself as legitimate athletic competition, but its closed structure has long encouraged suspicion. Wrestlers live in stables, travel together and remain within a small hierarchical world. Rank and income depend heavily on winning records. A wrestler with a secure majority of victories may face an opponent who desperately needs one final win to avoid demotion. To outsiders, the incentives for favors or arranged outcomes can seem obvious.

The allegations against Asashoryu were denied, and they were never established as fact. The Sumo Association and accused wrestlers pursued legal action, and Japanese courts later found the magazine’s reporting defamatory and ordered damages. It is therefore misleading to treat the bribery claims as proven misconduct.

But the allegations mattered even without proof. They gained traction because the association lacked credibility as an investigator of itself. Its instinct was to reject scandal as an attack on sumo’s honor rather than demonstrate, through independent scrutiny, that competition was clean.

That defensive culture would become even harder to sustain. In the same troubled period, sumo faced outrage over the fatal hazing of a young trainee at Tokitsukaze stable in 2007. Later scandals involving illegal gambling and, in 2011, documented match-fixing exposed through text messages confirmed that corruption was not merely a fantasy invented by hostile tabloids. Those later revelations did not validate every earlier accusation, and they did not prove the claims against Asashoryu. They did, however, show why blanket denials were insufficient.

## Tradition without accountability

Modern sumo’s core difficulty is not simply that it is old-fashioned. Its traditions are the source of its appeal: the rituals, clothing, stable life, ranking system and connection to Shinto give it a cultural depth unmatched by most professional sports.

The problem arises when tradition is used to resist accountability.

The Sumo Association historically operated as a self-governing fraternity of retired wrestlers. That arrangement preserved specialist knowledge, but it also encouraged secrecy and conflicts of interest. Stablemasters were responsible for developing athletes, enforcing discipline and protecting the reputation of the institution at the same time. Abuse could be dismissed as training, injuries concealed, and allegations investigated by people whose status depended on avoiding scandal.

Asashoryu’s case demonstrated the imbalance. The association could impose harsh discipline on an individual for embarrassing sumo, yet struggled to reassure the public about larger structural questions. It was decisive when defending etiquette, less convincing when defending competitive integrity or athlete welfare.

This distinction remains crucial. A sport can survive an ill-tempered champion. It cannot easily survive widespread doubt that its bouts are genuine, that its young wrestlers are safe or that its leaders are capable of policing themselves.

## The difficult legacy of Asashoryu

Asashoryu later returned to competition and continued winning championships, although further controversy eventually led to his retirement in 2010 after an alleged drunken assault. By then, his career had become inseparable from arguments about what a yokozuna should be and who had the authority to decide.

It would be easy to cast him as either villain or victim. Neither account is adequate.

He repeatedly showed poor judgment and often seemed unwilling to accept the symbolic obligations attached to his rank. At the same time, he was subjected to a level of scrutiny shaped by his foreignness, his dominance and the association’s need for a visible target. His successes were used to market sumo internationally; his failures were treated as proof that outsiders could not understand its spirit.

The central lesson of his career is that modern sumo cannot depend on moral symbolism alone. Invoking dignity does not replace clear rules. Punishing one champion does not address abusive training systems. Denying unsupported bribery allegations does not eliminate the need for independent oversight. Restricting foreign recruits does not solve declining domestic participation.

Asashoryu entered sumo in 1999 as evidence that the sport could renew itself by looking beyond Japan. His promotion to yokozuna in 2003 confirmed that talent could cross national boundaries. His suspension and the bribery allegations surrounding him then exposed an institution uncertain how to manage the world it had helped create.

Modern sumo’s challenge is therefore not to choose between tradition and change. It is to preserve the traditions that make the sport distinctive while abandoning the secrecy, inconsistency and insularity that make those traditions vulnerable. Asashoryu’s turbulent career remains the clearest warning of what happens when a global sport is governed as though it were still a closed village.
